extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media owners, press regulators and policy-makers concerned with press freedom and media policy in Jammu & Kashmir
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of the media environment, government media policy and administrative practices affecting news media operations, accreditation, advertising and safety of journalists in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empanelment requirement for government advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The Policy requires a newspaper or news platform to be 'empanelled' with the DIPR to be eligible to receive government advertising; for this the newspaper or news platform needs to be in continuous existence for a minimum period of 3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process of empanelment 'appears' to be gruelling; empanelment is a necessary condition but may not be sufficient for receiving ads. The report notes practical difficulties and delays in the empanelment process as a gatekeeping mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation principle: maximum reach and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The DIPR is to prepare media plans on the basis of maximum reach and economy when releasing government advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy mandates allocation by reach/economy and states newspapers cannot refuse to take advertising 'on pain of being de-empanelled.' The report highlights how this principle can be applied mechanistically or used to justify allocation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and non-support objective of government advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Government advertisement 'is not intended to provide financial support to any media... Promoting a transparent, constructive and healthy culture of unbiased information to all shall remain the overriding objective of the policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stated purpose should guide allocation decisions; the report contrasts the aspirational objective with ground realities where ads function as a major revenue source and suspension of ads effectively threatens outlets' survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited content/categories for ad release
rubrics_metrics.description: DIPR 'shall not release advertisements to such newspapers...which incite or tend to incite communal passions, preach violence, violate broad norms of public decency or carry out any acts or propagate any information prejudicial to the sovereignty and integrity of India.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy lists broad negative categories and explicitly invokes J&K's 'law and order and security' context; the report warns these categories allow wide subjective interpretation and can be used to exclude critical outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background/antecedent checks before empanelment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before empanelment, the 'antecedents of the paper/news portals as well that of its publishers / editors / key personnel are duly gone into.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy endorses vetting of personnel and organisations; the report flags this as a security-grounded provision that may be applied inconsistently or used to bar outlets based on political/editorial lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discrimination clause vs. practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy states that while releasing advertisements DIPR 'shall not take into account the political affiliation or editorial policies of the newspaper, publications and journals...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report evidence indicates selective withdrawal/curtailment of government advertising against outlets critical of administration (e.g., Greater Kashmir, Kashmir Reader), demonstrating a gap between the non-discrimination clause and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reasoned process for withdrawing/withholding ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Government/Information Department/ DIPR actions to suspend or withdraw advertising should be accompanied by reasons and follow a transparent, accountable process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report documents multiple cases where advertising was suspended or withdrawn without reasons given; editors reported no show-cause notices and appeals to authorities went unanswered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process for eviction/closure of government-allotted accommodation/offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ouster from government-allotted residential or office accommodation should follow due process, including written notice, show-cause procedures and judicial recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report describes summary sealing/eviction without written orders, denial of access to belongings and pending reimbursement for investments where courts quashed evictions—indicating procedural safeguards were not followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of journalists from arbitrary detention and criminalisation for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not be subjected to arbitrary summons, repeated interrogation, detention, or be charged under stringent laws for publishing news or social media posts without clear, lawful justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report lists numerous FIRs and charges (including under UAPA and PSA) against journalists and notes the chilling effect; it states there is 'no justification' for penalising journalists for legitimate reporting, though unlawful acts (arms, harbouring militants) are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and justification in use of security laws against media
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking security or stringent penal provisions (UAPA, PSA) against media persons requires clear evidence of unlawful activity rather than mere critical reporting or social media posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Gowhar Geelani, Masrat Zahra, Fahad Shah, Sajad Gul) illustrate where authorities invoked serious laws citing 'glorifying terrorism' or 'provoking people'—the report questions appropriateness and proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication access and non-discrimination in network restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions on internet and communication (e.g., prolonged shutdowns) should not unduly hobble journalists' ability to gather and transmit news; emergency measures must balance security and press functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report criticises prolonged internet shutdowns (e.g., two months from 5 August 2019) and describes the inadequate 'Media Facilitation Centre' with 4 (later 20) slow workstations, forcing journalists to use workarounds; such measures are judged to muzzle normal media functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation as a safeguard for journalists' movement and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Press accreditation is an important passport for safe passage and preventing harassment and detention when traveling in conflict zones; withholding fresh IDs impedes journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes press accreditation issuance stopped from 31 March 2020 with no fresh IDs, aggravating difficulties for reporters to access restricted areas and government offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government accountability to oversight inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities should respond to oversight bodies' (e.g., FFC/Press Council) requests for explanations about actions affecting journalists (e.g., ousters, arrests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FFC wrote formally to the Chief Secretary and sought responses about evictions and arrests; repeated non-response is recorded in the report as a failure of accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding economic coercion via advertising to influence editorial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of government advertising as a 'carrot-and-stick' to reward/penalise editorial lines is improper; allocation should not be used to throttle critical reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' depositions claim advertising powers were misused to discourage critical coverage, leading to layoffs and closures; the structural dependence on government ads in J&K makes this particularly harmful.
